item.title: GENTLEMEN RANSOMWARE LEAKS

item.title: How to respond to an incident in Kubernetes | GKE | Invictus Incident Response
item.description:
GKE provides better default logging than EKS with three log sources enabled out-of-the-box, but critical Data Access audit logs remain disabled by default and cannot be reconstructed post-incident.
Key IR considerations for GKE: • Standard vs Autopilot mode determines forensic capabilities - Autopilot blocks node-level access entirely • Data Access audit logs capture secret enumeration and kubectl exec activity but require pre-enabling • Default logs: Admin Activity (resource modifications), System Logs (container runtime), Application Logs (workload output) • Missing by default: API server logs, scheduler logs, controller manager logs, control plane network/SSH events • FluentBit vulnerability (GCP-2023-047) chained with Anthos Service Mesh permissions for cluster-admin escalation
Investigation approach: • Start with Cloud Logging filtered by affected node and timeframe • Query for unusual kubectl exec: `protoPayload.methodName="io.k8s.core.v1.Pod.exec"` • Quarantine compromised pods with deny-all NetworkPolicy while preserving for analysis • Remove pod labels to stop production traffic routing
Enable Data Access audit logs before incidents occur - they're the most valuable for investigations but cannot be retroactively enabled.

item.title: A Decade of BitLocker Vulnerabilities: What’s Patched, What’s Not, and What Still Works
item.description:

Key findings: • Microsoft's PCA 2011 certificate revocation (KB5025885) delayed until October 2026 expiry - most boot-chain attacks remain active • PIN+TPM defeats entire software toolchain and bus sniffing; only Intel PTT truly secure against public techniques • Default "Device Encryption" on Windows 11 Home/Pro remains trivially bypassable with USB stick
Hunt for WinRE tampering via reagentc /info output and check Secure Boot certificate trust with sigcheck bootmgfw.efi. Consider live memory acquisition priority over device shutdown.

item.title: Emulating & Exploiting UEFI: Unveiling Vulnerabilities in Firmware Security
item.description:
NetSPI researchers discover memory safety flaw in UEFI PNG decoder via emulation. Buffer over-read triggered by spoofed IDAT chunk length enables sensitive data leakage during boot process.
Key technical details: • Vulnerability bypasses LogoFail mitigations by manipulating PNG IDAT chunk length field to 0x400000 (4MB) while keeping total allocation under 0x7fffffff limit • Qiling framework emulation reveals over-read at instruction 0x104106: `mov al, byte ptr [r13+rcx]` attempting to access 0x9076000 when legitimate data ends at 0x9073B07 • Attack vector: crafted PNG loaded from NVRAM causes decoder to read beyond buffer boundaries into potentially sensitive memory regions • Custom heap spacing (0x10000000 bytes) in emulation environment isolates allocations to demonstrate clear evidence of boundary violations
DFIR artifacts: • Monitor UEFI boot logs for PNG processing errors or unexpected memory access violations • Examine NVRAM-stored image files for manipulated IDAT chunk headers during firmware forensics • Over-read could leak assembly code, cryptographic keys, or protected system data visible on screen during boot
Hunt for UEFI modules processing image data with insufficient boundary validation. Check PNG IDAT chunk lengths against actual compressed data size in firmware analysis.
